coherence.reasons: X sets four tests (affordability, like-for-like cost, reliability, robustness) and every later section answers one of them: the option matrix, the cost and sensitivity pages, the contingency, the cash bridge and the gates. Its executive summary maps one-to-one onto that body. Two wobbles: the headline year-end cash of ~$3.2M rests on a full-year 2027 operation X itself calls physically impossible, and the lease gate thresholds (208k, $84) come from a 2027-start lease although the lease would be triggered for 2028. Y is also orderly (economics, limits, delivery, recommendation), and its 2028-lease triggers (222k, $86.2) are consistent with the decision actually being deferred. But Y's summary opens with 'the owned cell saves $0.51M', a figure that depends on the non-binding resale, and then rejects that option. That makes its top-line logic less direct than X's 'own is $1.6M dearer unless resale is realised'.

judgment.reasons: Both reach the key's preferred answer: keep buying, add a second source and reserved capacity, hold the lease as a gated option, reject the owned cell. X weighs the trade-offs more fully. It scores each option against the four tests with explicit pass, partial or fail, and admits its own recommendation is only partial on reliability and robustness. It separates prerequisites (site survey, spec frozen, ≥94% yield proven at full speed) from switch triggers (volume, price, two quarters under 97%). It states when the owned cell could be revisited (financing, committed volume, proven scrap, binding resale) and shows cash headroom if the lease is triggered. Y's three triggers are sound, correctly recomputed for a 2028 start, and carry a decision deadline of end-September 2027. But Y has no process-proof gate, its delivery trigger has no duration, and it gives no revisit conditions for the owned cell. Y's observation that a single cell would need a backup too is a good point that X does not make explicitly.

evidence.reasons: Both are numerically sound where I checked them. Both get $75 delivered, $47.92 and $50.00 per good unit, and three-year totals of 22.50 / 22.20 / 24.09 (21.99 with resale). X's 207k break-even and Y's 287k are the same calculation on different bases. X's paybacks (3.7 and 7.2 years), 279k owned-cell payback volume and sensitivity cases all check out, as do Y's 78% capital recovery, 222k, $86.2 and 183k. X's weaknesses: it headlines ~$3.2M year-end cash instead of the key's $1.9M (which it gives only in a footnote), and its gate thresholds use a 2027-start basis. Y's weaknesses: its headline owned-cell saving ($1.70 per unit, $0.51M) depends on the non-binding resale, though it flags that, and it has far less sensitivity testing. Y makes one sharp catch X misses: the 96.8% is measured on orders while the contract counts requested units. X uses the critical evidence more thoroughly: partial-year start-up, price sensitivity, supplier price exposure per $1, a carrying-cost estimate, the effect of discounting, and a claim-by-claim rebuttal table. X also leads with the no-resale comparison the key treats as primary.

revision.reasons: The pack's initial hypothesis is the VP of Operations' call to build an owned cell because $46 beats $75; the key expects it rejected. Both reject it on the capital cap, the cash floor and the unit mismatch. X is more complete. It rebuts five circulating claims by name: the VP's $46-versus-$75 claim, the CFO's $27 and payback, the 98.5% yield, the machine-shop correlation, and the VP's 'buy capacity early for 2029' argument. It shows the owned cell costs $80.31 per good unit against $75 and fails all four tests. Its 'our starting hypothesis, a leased cell' is a team hypothesis not in the pack, but it is tested honestly and does not displace the handling of the VP's position. Y rejects the owned cell and corrects the CFO slide, the demo yield and the correlation. It does not address the VP's 2029 lead-time argument directly, and its headline that the owned cell still 'saves $0.51M' with resale softens the rejection relative to the key's view that fully loaded costs make it dearer than buying.

overall.reasons: Both documents would lead the committee to the same defensible decision with correct core numbers. X serves the CEO's four requests more completely. It gives the recommendation, a cash bridge with headroom even if the lease is triggered, a fuller gate set including process proof at full speed, and a five-layer contingency with costs, timings and owners. It also tests whether the lease's 1% edge survives volume, price, scrap and start-up timing. Y is tighter and has two points X lacks: the orders-versus-units measurement basis and thresholds computed for a 2028-start lease. But it is thinner on sensitivities and gate design, and its framing of the owned cell leans on the non-binding resale. X's flaws (the ~$3.2M headline cash figure and gate thresholds on a 2027-start basis) do not change the decision.
